lead: A prestressed beam must pass two different tests. Before it carries service load, the jacking force and self-weight must not overstress the concrete. Under full load, the effective prestress and the loads must keep tension within the chosen class. At collapse, the tendon stress rises far above the effective prestress, and the section must have enough ultimate moment. Design therefore chooses a section and tendon, checks transfer and service stresses, then checks ultimate flexure. The same sequence is used for a roof beam, a bridge girder or a precast slab.
prereq: You need: 6.4 for stress calculation and 6.5 for effective prestress, plus the limit state flexure stress block from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Service stress checks set the section

blocks.text: Every prestressed flexural member is checked at two stages. At transfer, when the tendon is released, the force is the initial prestress P<sub>i</sub> and the only load is self-weight. At service, the force is the effective prestress P<sub>e</sub> = P<sub>i</sub> minus losses, and the load is the full service load. Extreme fibre stresses are found by adding axial, prestress bending and load bending.

blocks.where: f is stress in N/mm², compression positive; P is prestress force in N; A is concrete area in mm²; e is tendon eccentricity from the centroid in mm; Z = I/y is the section modulus in mm³; M is bending moment in Nmm; the ± signs follow the fibre and the tendon side.

blocks.text: At transfer the concrete is young, so the code allows a lower compressive stress, often written as a fraction of the cube strength at transfer f<sub>ci</sub>. At service the limit is a fraction of the characteristic cube strength f<sub>ck</sub>. These limits stop crushing and excessive creep.

Tension is controlled by choosing a behaviour class. Type 1: no tension at service, used for liquid-retaining tanks and aggressive exposure. Type 2: tension allowed but below the modulus of rupture, so no visible crack, used for bridge decks. Type 3: cracks allowed but width limited by ordinary reinforcement, used in partially prestressed members (see 6.9). Some syllabi and IS 1343 call these Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3. Section size is often governed by the transfer check, not by ultimate strength: a beam strong enough at collapse may still crush at release because Pi acts on a small concrete area.

At ultimate, the concrete cracks and the tendon stress is no longer P<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>p</sub>. For bonded tendons the strain is compatible with the surrounding concrete, so the tendon stress rises to f<sub>pb</sub>. Codes give f<sub>pb</sub> from tables using the ultimate tendon strength f<sub>pu</sub>, concrete strength f<sub>ck</sub> and effective prestress. For a rectangular section with only bonded tendons, horizontal equilibrium gives:

blocks.where: f<sub>ck</sub> is characteristic cube strength in N/mm²; b is section width in mm; x<sub>u</sub> is neutral axis depth in mm; A<sub>p</sub> is tendon area in mm²; f<sub>pb</sub> is tendon stress at ultimate in N/mm².
M<sub>u</sub> is ultimate moment in Nmm; d is effective depth to the tendon centroid in mm; the lever arm is d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>. Compare M<sub>u</sub> with the factored design moment.

blocks.text: For a flanged section, if x<sub>u</sub> lies within the flange, use b = b<sub>f</sub>. If x<sub>u</sub> is below the flange, C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>w</sub> x<sub>u</sub> + 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> (b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>) D<sub>f</sub>, where b<sub>w</sub> is web width in mm, b<sub>f</sub> is flange width in mm and D<sub>f</sub> is flange thickness in mm; equate this C to A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub>. Mild steel can be added: 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> = A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> + 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>s</sub>, with its moment 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>s</sub> (d<sub>s</sub> − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>), where d<sub>s</sub> is effective depth to the rebar. Shear and deflection are separate checks: shear reinforcement from Unit 3, deflection from Unit 2 serviceability. Flexural design only fixes the section and tendon for moment.

examples.question: A rectangular pretensioned beam has width b = 300 mm, effective depth d = 700 mm and bonded tendon area A<sub>p</sub> = 500 mm². The tendon stress at ultimate is f<sub>pb</sub> = 1500 N/mm² and the concrete cube strength is f<sub>ck</sub> = 50 N/mm². Find the neutral axis depth x<sub>u</sub> and the ultimate moment M<sub>u</sub>.
steps: Tension at ultimate: T = A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> = 500 × 1500 = 750,000 N.
Concrete compression: C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> = 0.36 × 50 × 300 × x<sub>u</sub> = 5400 x<sub>u</sub> N.
Equate T and C: 5400 x<sub>u</sub> = 750,000, so x<sub>u</sub> = 138.9 mm.
examples.answer: x<sub>u</sub> = 138.9 mm and M<sub>u</sub> = 481.25 kNm, about 481 kNm.
examples.check:
b = 300
d = 700
Ap = 500
fpb = 1500
fck = 50
T = Ap * fpb
xu = T / (0.36 * fck * b)
lever = d - 0.42 * xu
Mu_kNm = T * lever / 1e6
print(round(xu, 1))
print(round(Mu_kNm, 2))

traps: Using the effective prestress force P<sub>e</sub> as the ultimate capacity. Ultimate tension is A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub>, and f<sub>pb</sub> is much larger than P<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>p</sub>.
Forgetting that transfer uses P<sub>i</sub> and self-weight only, while service uses P<sub>e</sub> and full load. Losses change the force and the stress sign.
A sign slip: a tendon below the centroid causes hogging, so it adds compression at the bottom and tension at the top. Locate the tendon side before adding moments.
Using the full flange width b<sub>f</sub> in 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> when x<sub>u</sub> is below the flange. Below the flange, compression uses the web plus the flange overhang.
Unit slip: f in N/mm² and dimensions in mm give M in Nmm. Divide by 10⁶ for kNm; a missing factor of 10⁶ makes the answer look 1000 times too large.

quiz.q: What is f<sub>pb</sub> in prestressed flexural design?
quiz.a: The stress in the tendon at the ultimate limit state, taken from code tables using f<sub>pu</sub>, f<sub>ck</sub> and effective prestress. It is not the effective prestress.

quiz.q: Why can a beam pass the ultimate moment check but fail the transfer stress check?
quiz.a: At transfer the initial prestress P<sub>i</sub> acts on young concrete of small area, giving high compressive stress. Ultimate strength depends on A<sub>p</sub> f<sub>pb</sub> and d, not on this early stress. Transfer often governs the section size.

quiz.q: Name the three behaviour classes for tension under service load.
quiz.a: Type 1: no tension. Type 2: tension allowed but below modulus of rupture, no visible crack. Type 3: cracks allowed but width controlled by ordinary reinforcement. Some syllabi and IS 1343 call these Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3.

quiz.q: A rectangular bonded section has b = 250 mm, d = 600 mm, A<sub>p</sub> = 400 mm², f<sub>pb</sub> = 1400 N/mm² and f<sub>ck</sub> = 45 N/mm². Find x<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub>.
A Type 2 member has calculated extreme fibre tension 4.2 N/mm² at service, but the modulus of rupture is 3.5 N/mm². What do you conclude?
quiz.a: The tension exceeds the modulus of rupture, so the section will crack and does not satisfy Type 2 behaviour. Revise the section or tendon to reduce tension, or design it as Type 3 with crack-width control.

quiz.q: Why is f<sub>pb</sub> greater than the stress P<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>p</sub> in a bonded tendon?
quiz.a: At ultimate the concrete cracks and strains increase. Bond forces the tendon strain to increase with the concrete, so the tendon stress rises toward f<sub>pu</sub>. The effective prestress is only the service-stage stress.

quiz.q: A T-section has b<sub>f</sub> = 900 mm, b<sub>w</sub> = 300 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 120 mm and x<sub>u</sub> = 200 mm. Write the concrete compression force.
quiz.a: Since x<sub>u</sub> > D<sub>f</sub>, C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>w</sub> x<sub>u</sub> + 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> (b<sub>f</sub> − b<sub>w</sub>) D<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> (300 × 200) + 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> (600 × 120) = (21,600 + 32,400) f<sub>ck</sub> = 54,000 f<sub>ck</sub> N.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, designers use spreadsheets or finite element models to iterate section, tendon profile and jacking force before drawing the tendon. Site measurements of friction and anchorage slip update the loss calculation, and the transfer stress is checked against the actual cube strength at release. Modern codes increasingly use strain-compatibility analysis for unbonded and external tendons. Search terms: IS 1343 flexural design, ACI 318 prestressed ultimate moment, strain compatibility unbonded tendon, prestress transfer stress limits.
